Write a short blog post about battling weeds. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the post only.
final_message:
The weeds came up again this morning, as they do every morning, with the cheerful air of people who have been invited. I went out at six, with my coffee and a high resolve, and by seven I had pulled out enough purslane to stuff a mattress. By noon it had all come back. I do not say this to complain; I say it to establish the facts, which are that the weed is a creature of perfect industry and I am not.

There is a theory, held by the neighbors, that a weed is merely a plant out of place. This is a comfortable doctrine, and I notice it is held chiefly by those whose own gardens are somewhere else. In mine, the plant is never out of place. It is exactly where it wishes to be, which is between the lettuce and the sun. The lettuce, I am sorry to say, has no opinions on the matter, and yields the ground without a struggle.

Polly says I should mulch. She says it as one might say, "You should be taller." Mulch is excellent in the abstract. You spread it a few inches deep, and the weeds, finding the situation dark and damp, are supposed to give it up and go elsewhere. But I have seen a dandelion come up through a board walk, and look about it with a kind of mild surprise, as if wondering why anybody had put a board there. Against such a character, a little straw is not an argument.

I have tried the hoe, and the hoe is honest work. There is a particular satisfaction in the clean stroke that takes off a thistle at the neck, and leaves it lying in the sun to think over its conduct. This is the best part of the whole business. It lasts perhaps four minutes. Then you look up, and discover that you have been standing in a row of its relations, who are all in blossom, and who all seem quite pleased to see you.

I once consulted a book on the subject, written by a man who had, I think, never kept a garden, or had kept it only through a window. He advised "vigilance, patience, and a regular system." I have the vigilance; the weeds have the system. They are on the regular plan of coming up everywhere at once, and it is a plan against which no mere vigilance has ever prevailed.

And yet I would not give it up. There is something in the contest which does one good: the early air, the damp earth, the sudden bird on the fence-post, who has come to see how I am getting on and who, I think, is not unamused. If the weeds should ever be wholly beaten, I suppose I should have to take up something worse, such as politics. So I go out again tomorrow, with the hoe, and the coffee, and a great deal less resolve.
